items.title: 10.10.2 Calculating the charge on an electron

source_refs.note: Topic 10.10.2 with Quick Check 10.5, printed pages 223-224.

blocks.text: A sample calculation is shown below, using a current of 0.20 A for 34 min.

blocks.latex: \text{mass of anode at start of the experiment} = 56.53\ \text{g}
blocks.text_alt: mass of anode at start of the experiment = 56.53 g

blocks.latex: \text{mass of anode at end of experiment} = 56.40\ \text{g}
blocks.text_alt: mass of anode at end of experiment = 56.40 g
mass of copper removed from anode = 0.13 g

blocks.latex: \text{quantity of charge passed } Q = I \times t = 0.20 \times 34 \times 60 = 408\ \text{C}
blocks.text_alt: quantity of charge passed Q = I × t = 0.20 × 34 × 60 = 408 C

blocks.text: As the amount of copper removed is 0.13 g

blocks.text_alt: So, 0.13 g of copper requires = 408 C

blocks.text: But the equation for the electrolysis shows that 2 moles of electrons are needed to produce 1 mole of copper:

blocks.text_alt: The charge on 1 mole of electrons = (63.5 / 0.13) × 408 C = 99646 C

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed working gives 408 / 0.13 × 63.5 = 99646 C for 63.5 g of copper; the product is 199292 C. That is the charge for 1 mole of copper, which needs 2 moles of electrons, so the charge on 1 mole of electrons is 199292 / 2 = 99646 C (and 63.5 / 0.13 × 408 C is also 199292 C, not 99646 C). The value of L below is unchanged.
If the charge on one electron is 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C,
This is in good agreement with the accurate value of 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
